title: Tengri and the Making of the World
source_ref: The Secret History of the Mongols (13th century); Orkhon Turkic inscriptions (732-735 CE); Mongol shamanic invocations recorded in the 19th-20th centuries
paragraphs: Tengri is the sky, the oldest power on the steppe. Turkic inscriptions from the eighth century set the blue heaven above and the brown earth below, with human beings between them. The Secret History of the Mongols opens in the same key: a blue-grey wolf born of heaven, a fallow doe, and later a shining light that enters a woman's tent. Heaven is the source of life and authority.

The inscriptions do not tell a creation story. They say that Tengri, the earth and the waters stood behind the Turkic khaganate and gave the khan his mandate. Bilge Kagan calls himself 'Tengri-like and Tengri-born'. Umay, the goddess of children and the womb, appears in the same inscriptions as a mother-like power. Heaven, earth and water are invoked together as one ordered world that upholds a ruler and a people.

No single creation narrative survives. One Turkic account has a white goose over endless water; a voice called Ak Ana, the White Mother, tells it to create, and the first being it makes turns away and becomes a rival. Mongol shamanic invocations speak of Mongke Tngri, Eternal Heaven, and later Buddhist chronicles rewrite the beginning in Buddhist terms. Buryat and Altai stories add a creator, a water bird, or a primordial pair.

Order, in these accounts, is not finished once. The sky is tiered, and the ninety-nine tngri are counted as fifty-five white and forty-four black, in western and eastern companies. The earth has its mistresses, the seventy-seven natigai, and Umay watches hearth and newborn. Human life is held between them. People offer milk, tea and meat at ovoos, and the shaman calls the tngri only for the gravest matters.
notes: No single creation narrative survives. This retelling combines the Orkhon inscriptions, the opening of the Secret History and later Mongol shamanic invocations, which were recorded in the 19th and 20th centuries. The white-goose and Ak Ana episode belongs to one Turkic account, not to all Turkic or Mongol traditions; the 99 tngri and 77 natigai are scholarly counts drawn mainly from Heissig and Hesse, and local lists differ. Buddhist chronicles from the 17th century onward reshape the material again.

title: Geser Khan
source_ref: Mongolian Geser (Beijing woodblock, 1716); Buryat Geser epic, recorded in the 19th-20th centuries; Tibetan Gesar epic
paragraphs: Geser is a heavenly hero, and the world he enters is out of joint. In the Buryat prologue, the sky god Khormusta defeats the demon Atai Ulan and scatters his body across the earth; its pieces become monsters. The heavenly middle son is sent down to repair the damage. Tibetan and Mongol versions begin differently, but all agree that a divine power takes birth among people to restore order.

His birth is miraculous and his childhood lowly. In the Mongol version he is born to a human mother after a heavenly sign, and grows up ugly, snotty and mocked. In the Tibetan epic his mother conceives him through a magic drink or a vision in water. He wins a horse race, marries the princess and takes the throne of Ling. The despised boy is revealed as the king.

His wars are against demons, not ordinary enemies. He defeats the many-headed mangus, the demon kings of the north and the monsters born from Atai Ulan's blood. In the Mongol version he also unmasks a demon disguised as a lama, and in one episode he descends to the underworld to rescue his mother. His horse, his armour and his companions come to him through feats that mark him as chosen.

Victory is never final. Enemies return, the world forgets its lessons, and Geser is betrayed or wearied. In many tellings he withdraws to a hidden realm, promising to return when needed. The epic crosses borders: Tibetan, Mongol, Buryat, Oirat, Ladakhi and Balti versions differ, and the first printed text was a Mongolian woodblock of 1716, not a Tibetan original. Buddhist, Bon and shamanic elements meet in it.
notes: The Geser epic exists in Tibetan, Mongol, Buryat, Oirat, Ladakhi, Balti and other versions, and they disagree about Geser's parentage, his wife's name, the number of his campaigns and his ending. The Buryat prologue with Khormusta and Atai Ulan is not in the Tibetan versions, and the descent to rescue his mother is a Mongol episode. The 1716 Beijing woodblock is the earliest printed text, not the original. This composite follows the Mongol and Buryat outlines and should not be read as one canonical epic.

title: Manas
source_ref: Manas epic, Kyrgyz trilogy (Manas, Semetey, Seytek), as performed by manaschi; written records from Valikhanov (1856) onward
paragraphs: Manas is sung, not read. A manaschi performs the epic from memory in a rhythmic chant, without an instrument, and a full telling can last for nights. There is no single authorised text. Each singer shapes the story with formulaic epithets, repeated scenes and genealogies, and the trilogy continues through Manas's son Semetey and his grandson Seytek. Dozens of written versions of parts of the epic exist.

His father Jakyp has herds but no heir. He prays and gives alms, and a son is born; a foal born the same day is set aside for the boy. Manas grows fast, strong and unruly, and the Oirats, alarmed by reports of him, try to capture him. He escapes, gathers followers and is proclaimed khan. The epic remembers this as the beginning of a long campaign to unite the Kyrgyz tribes.

His companions are the forty choro, and among them Almambet, a prince from China whose mother was Kyrgyz, who leaves his father's court and becomes Manas's sworn brother. Kanikey, daughter of the khan of Bukhara and Manas's wife, is the epic's sharpest mind: she advises him, guards his household and later hides Semetey from his enemies. In one tradition she orders a false inscription on his tomb.

Manas unites the Kyrgyz, or in older versions the Nogais, and leads them back from the Altai to the mountains of Kyrgyzstan. He fights the Oirats, the Uyghurs and the Afghans, and his campaigns end in alliances as often as victories. His death is told variously: in many performances he is wounded through treachery and the story passes to Semetey. Scholars place the epic's events anywhere from the ninth to the eighteenth century.
notes: Manas is oral and formulaic, and no two manaschi tell it alike. This retelling follows the widely known outline: Jakyp's late heir, the forty choro, Almambet, Kanikey, the return from the Altai and the wars with the Oirats. The epic's historical setting is disputed, with dates from the 9th to the 18th century proposed, and 19th-century versions make Manas a leader of the Nogais while later versions make him the Kyrgyz national hero. The mausoleum at Talas bears an inscription to Kenizek-Khatun, which legend explains as Kanikey's ruse.

title: The Swan Maiden and Bayan Khongor
source_ref: Buryat Khori swan-maiden legend (Khoridoy Mergen), recorded in the 19th-20th centuries; Mongol versions of ATU 400
paragraphs: A hunter named Bayan Khongor rides the shore of Lake Baikal and sees nine swans settle on the water. They shed their feathers and become young women, daughters of a heavenly father. While they bathe, he hides one garment. The others put on their feathers and fly away; the youngest cannot. She stays, naked and calling, and he offers her a home and a hearth.

She agrees, and for years they live well. He keeps the feathered robe hidden, and she bears eleven sons, the ancestors of the Khori clans. She sews their coats, tends the fire and says nothing about the sky. But when the cranes and swans fly south, she grows quiet. At last she asks to see her old clothes once, only to look at them, and he cannot refuse her.

She puts on the robe and becomes a swan. She rises through the smoke-hole of the yurt, and as he catches at her feet he leaves a smear of clay on them; that is why swans have black legs, the Buryats say. Before she goes she names and blesses her sons: let them live in peace and increase. Then she is gone, and the hunter is left with eleven boys and a story.

The tale is classified as ATU 400, the swan-maiden bride, and told from Ireland to Manchuria. In Buryat versions the woman is an ancestress, not a captive; the Khori honour swans, sprinkle milk after them and refuse to kill them. The hunter's name varies, and the story is also told of Khoridoy Mergen and Hori Tumed. The theft of the robe remains the hinge, and modern tellers do not hide its cruelty.
notes: This retelling uses Bayan Khongor as the hunter's name; the recorded Buryat versions usually call him Khoridoy Mergen, Hori Tumed or Baragutai, and Bayan Khongor is also the name of a mountain in Buryatia. The number of swans (three, nine or thirteen), the number of sons (eleven or thirteen), the way the robe is recovered and the ending vary. ATU 400 is a folktale classification, not a single text, and the story is also told well beyond the steppe.

title: Erlik and the Underworld
source_ref: Orkhon inscriptions (8th century); Altai and Khakas epic and shamanic texts recorded in the 19th-20th centuries; Mongol Geser and Buryat materials
paragraphs: Erlik rules the dead. The name is Turkic, and Mongol speakers call him Erleg; the Orkhon inscriptions already know a lord of the underworld. He is not a simple devil. In Altai accounts he is a brother or rival of the sky god, a cosmic power with his own realm, his own palace and his own justice. He sends sickness and death, and he keeps the souls that come to him.

His realm lies in Tamag, reached through a stone opening, a cave or a river. It has an iron wall, a copper palace and a court of judgement. Erlik has nine sons and nine daughters; his daughters try to distract the shaman climbing to the upper world. He is feared but also addressed: people sacrifice to him when sickness strikes, because a power that takes life can also be persuaded to return it.

Heroes go down to him. In the Mongol Geser, the hero descends to the underworld to bring back his mother, and in Turkic epic a champion may follow a stolen soul into Erlik's country. The journey is a sequence of thresholds, each with a guardian and a demand. The hero wins by courage, by cunning or by accepting help from the dead, and returns changed.

Erlik is not only a threat. He belongs to a world that is complete only with him: the upper sky, the middle earth and the lower realm are parts of one order, and the dead have their own place in it. Modern communities disagree about how far he should be honoured, and Buddhist and Muslim writers have recast him in their own terms. The old stories do not resolve the question.
notes: Erlik's character varies greatly. The Orkhon inscriptions mention a lord of the underworld, but the detailed pictures come from Altai, Khakas and other Siberian Turkic materials recorded in the 19th and 20th centuries, where Erlik is a brother or rival of the sky god. Mongol Erleg and Buddhist-influenced accounts differ, and Muslim Turkic traditions often recast him. The descent in the Mongol Geser is one epic episode, not a universal shamanic rite, and the retelling keeps the cosmic role without making him a simple devil.

title: The Shaman's Journey
source_ref: Ethnographic accounts of Mongol and Buryat shamanism (19th-20th centuries); living Buryat and Mongolian practice; Heissig, Humphrey and others
paragraphs: The drum is the shaman's horse. It is made of hide stretched over a wooden hoop, painted with spirits and animals, and hung with metal discs that ring as the shaman moves. In Mongol and Buryat practice drum, costume and staff are not props but vehicles that carry the shaman out of ordinary space. The drumming begins slowly, then settles into a steady beat that can last for hours.

The ascent goes up a ladder of worlds. The shaman names the sky's layers, calls the ancestral spirits and the tngri, and climbs toward the highest heaven, where Mongke Tngri or Qormusta Tengri holds the order of the world. Not every journey reaches the top. In many traditions the shaman stops at a lower heaven and speaks through an intermediary, because the highest power is not approached directly.

The descent goes the other way, to Erlik or to the land of the dead, to find a soul that has strayed or been taken. The shaman passes guardians, offers what they ask and returns with the soul or with the knowledge needed. The return is the point of the journey: healing, a restored household, a death properly mourned. A journey that does not return is a danger the stories know.

Practice varies, and much is not shown to outsiders. Buryat shamans may be Buddhist as well, honouring both datsan and ovoo; Mongolian shamans distinguish black and yellow traditions; Kyrgyz and Kazakh healers work inside Muslim communities. Soviet campaigns killed and imprisoned shamans; Chinese campaigns suppressed ritual in Inner Mongolia. Since the 1990s people have rebuilt lineages, argued over authenticity and gone online. Initiation is not a secret this retelling reveals.
notes: Ethnographic descriptions of shamanic journeys differ by community, and some ritual knowledge is not meant for publication. This retelling draws on published Mongol and Buryat accounts and on living practice, but it does not describe initiation, and it should not be used as a ritual manual. Soviet and Chinese repression, Buddhist and Muslim influence, and the post-1990 revival have all reshaped what is practised and what is told. Terms such as shaman, healer and spirit-master are not exact equivalents.
